name: Critical thinking
draftedBy: Claude, 15 Nov 2026, from Bryan's entry 1 in docs/VOID_UNIVERSITY.md (13 Oct 2026). Every line here waits for Bryan to keep, change or strike.
why: Most of what reaches you every day is somebody's claim: an ad, a post, a doctor's pamphlet, a boss, a news story, a relative at dinner. Nobody can check everything, so the skill is knowing which claims to trust, which to test, and how. People who never learn it spend their money, their votes and their health on other people's say-so.
outcomes: Tell a claim from its evidence.
Spot the standard ways an argument cheats.
Know what a number can and cannot say.
Notice when a story is doing the thinking for you.
Change your mind in public without shame.
Read a hard text without an intermediary telling you what it means.

units.title: A claim is not its evidence
units.outcome: Tell a claim from its evidence.
units.why: Before you can weigh anything, you have to see that "this works" and "here is how we know" are two different things. Most people hear the first and assume the second.
units.reachesYou: Supplements, miracle cleaners, "studies show", the phone call that says your car warranty is expiring. Each one is a claim asking for your money before it shows its evidence.

main.title: Secrets of the Psychics
main.licence: No licence stated; an Archive upload of the broadcast, the same footing as VoidTV's shows.
main.note: A stage magician tests faith healers, spoon benders and astrologers by setting up fair tests, not by arguing. Watch how each test is built.

companions.title: The Ethics of Belief, part 1: The Duty of Inquiry
companions.by: W. K. Clifford (1877), read for LibriVox
companions.note: The shipowner who believed his ship was sound. A short, sharp argument that believing without evidence is a wrong done to other people.

companions.title: Cosmos, episode 3: Harmony of the Worlds
companions.file: Cosmos - A Personal Voyage - ep 3 - Harmony of the Worlds (ABC Australia 1984 Broadcast).mp4
companions.note: Astrology and astronomy started as one thing. Sagan shows the moment they split: Kepler threw away his own beautiful theory because eight minutes of arc did not fit the data.

units.do: Pick one claim you heard this week. Write the claim on one line and its evidence on the next. If the second line is empty, that is your answer.

partials: Peter Popoff named strangers' illnesses on stage. Randi found the radio in his ear.
Kepler threw out his own beautiful theory over eight minutes of arc.
Clifford's shipowner was sure his ship was sound. It sank.
The label says clinically proven.
Astrology and astronomy began as one subject.
crystal.key: A claim earns belief only from a test it could have failed.

decoys.text: Trust whoever is most sure of themselves.
decoys.why: Popoff was completely sure. Certainty is a feeling, not a test.

decoys.text: If smart people believe it, it is probably true.
decoys.why: Kepler was brilliant and his first theory was wrong. Smart people need the test too.

crystal.aha: Every partial here is a test someone ran, or refused to run.

beats.say: So you don't pay. Not yet.
Every claim works the same way.
No evidence? Don't buy it yet.

units.needIt: Every ad, sales pitch and viral post hands you a claim; asking "how do we know?" before you buy, share or vote keeps your money and your name safe.

units.title: How an argument cheats
units.outcome: Spot the standard ways an argument cheats.
units.why: The tricks are old and there are not many of them. Once you can name them, they stop working on you, and you stop using them by accident.
units.reachesYou: Sales pitches, arguments at work, comment threads, family fights, political ads. The same few moves show up in all of them.

main.title: The Art of Controversy: Stratagems 1 to 10
main.by: Arthur Schopenhauer (written about 1831), read for LibriVox
main.note: Schopenhauer wrote down, plainly and a little cynically, the tricks people use to win an argument when they are wrong. Stratagems 11 to 38 follow in the next parts.

companions.title: The Art of Controversy: Stratagems 11 to 20
On Bullshit
companions.licence: In copyright: we point you to a library copy rather than an upload.
companions.note: A short essay with an exact distinction: a liar cares about the truth enough to hide it; a bullshitter does not care either way.

units.do: Watch any panel show or comment thread for ten minutes and name three of Schopenhauer's stratagems by number when you catch them.

partials: Stretch the other person's claim until it breaks (stratagem 1).
Make them angry, because angry people argue badly (stratagem 8).
Call it by a name that already judges it (stratagem 12).
A bullshitter does not care whether it is true.
Answer a different question from the one that was asked.
crystal.key: These moves work on the person, not on the question.

decoys.text: Whoever wins the argument was right.
decoys.why: Schopenhauer wrote the tricks down because the winner is so often wrong.
Frankfurt's point is that most of it comes from not caring, and anyone does it when cornered.

crystal.aha: Once you see the move is aimed at the person, it stops working on you.

map: the loud part of the argument
your point changed into a weaker one
the straw man they knock down

beats.say: The ball goes under the middle cup.
While you listen, the cups swap.
You point to the middle. Empty.
Watch the claim, not the talk.

units.needIt: Arguments at work, at home and online are often won by tricks instead of reasons; spotting the trick lets you answer the point and not the pressure.

units.title: What a number can and cannot say
units.outcome: Know what a number can and cannot say.
units.why: Numbers sound like the end of an argument. They are usually the start of one: who counted, what they counted, and compared with what.
units.reachesYou: Interest rates, "cuts your risk by half", crime up 200 percent, a raise that is smaller than prices went up. Your money and your health decisions come wrapped in numbers.

main.title: The best stats you've ever seen
main.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 (TED). Credit TED and Hans Rosling; no edits.
main.note: A doctor who worked in Mozambique shows that what most educated people believe about the world is decades out of date, and how one chart fixes it.

companions.title: The magic washing machine
companions.note: Nine minutes on what one machine did for his mother, and what energy numbers mean in a real home.

companions.title: Don't Panic: The Truth About Population
companions.licence: No licence stated; an Archive mirror of the broadcast.
companions.note: The hour-long version, for when the talk hooks you.

companions.title: The Ethics of Belief, part 3: The Limits of Inference
companions.by: W. K. Clifford (1877), read for LibriVox
companions.note: When are we allowed to believe beyond what we have seen?

companions.title: How to Lie with Statistics
companions.licence: In copyright: we point you to a library copy rather than an upload.

units.do: Find one percentage in today's news. Ask three questions of it: a percent of what, compared with what, and who counted.

partials: Most educated people think the world is poorer and sicker than it is.
One washing machine gave Rosling's mother hours back every week.
"Cuts your risk in half" can mean 2 in a million down to 1 in a million.
An average can hide that most people are below it.
Clifford: we may believe past what we have seen only by assuming the unseen is like the seen.
crystal.key: A number means nothing until you know: of what, compared with what, and who counted.

decoys.why: A number can't lie, but whoever chose which number to show you can.

decoys.text: A bigger number means a bigger problem.
decoys.why: 200 percent of a tiny thing is still tiny. Compared with what?

crystal.aha: Every number above changed meaning the moment you asked what it was compared with.

scene.analogy: A sale price after the price went up

beats.say: Every big number works this way.

lab.title: The chance machine
lab.ask: Every ball is one thing counted. Every peg is a bit of chance that nudges it. Change how many you count and how the board sits, and watch what the pile can and cannot tell you.

rules.if: you count only 10 on a level board, and then count 10 again,
rules.then: the pile changes shape every time. A small count can say almost anything.

rules.if: you count 500 on a level board,
rules.then: a hill appears with its top on the middle. Do it again and you get the same hill. Counting many is what makes a number steady.

rules.if: you tilt the board and count 500,
rules.then: the whole hill moves over, smooth and sure of itself. Counting more did not fix it. A crooked way of counting stays crooked at any size.

rules.if: you tilt the board and count only 10,
rules.then: it looks like any other small pile. Look at your level tries: they were lopsided too. A small count cannot even show you the board is crooked.

map: one person asked, one thing counted
lab.meet: Where you meet this: a product rated 5 stars by 9 buyers. A poll of people who chose to answer. "Works for 4 out of 5", of how many? Ask how many were counted, and how they were picked.
lab.draftedBy: Claude, 15 Nov 2026: a draft for Bryan to keep, change or strike.

units.needIt: Loan rates, medical risks and "50% off" are all numbers someone chose to show you; three quick questions tell you whether they mean what they seem to.

scale.title: The weight of everything alive
scale.ask: Each block is one group of living things, and its volume is that group's real share of all life on Earth. Guess first, then turn it, zoom in, and walk down the row until you find the people.

states.name: Before people spread
states.note: The paper's rough numbers for the world before the great loss of large animals (which began about 50,000 years ago) and before farming. A faint outline means the paper gives no number for then, so today's size is kept.

things.name: Plants
things.more: Mostly trees, and mostly wood. The paper says plants have fallen to about half since people began clearing land.

things.name: Bacteria
things.more: Most of them live deep underground. This number is sure only to within about ten times.

things.name: Fungi
things.more: Mushrooms are the small part you see; most of it is threads in the soil.

things.name: Archaea
things.more: Single cells much like bacteria, mostly deep underground.

things.name: Protists
things.more: Algae, amoebas and other single cells that have a nucleus.

things.name: Sea arthropods
things.more: Krill, crabs, shrimp and the tiny copepods that fill the oceans.

things.name: Fish
things.more: Fishing has taken about 100 million tonnes out of the total.

things.name: Land arthropods
things.more: Insects, spiders and their kin.

things.name: Worms
things.more: Earthworms and the other segmented worms (annelids).

things.name: Molluscs
things.more: Snails, clams, squid.

things.name: Viruses
things.more: Counted by the paper beside the living things. Sure only to within about twenty times.

things.name: Livestock
things.more: Farm mammals, mostly cattle and pigs.

things.name: Roundworms
things.more: Nematodes: more of them by count than any other animal, and still this small.

things.name: Wild mammals
things.more: Every wild mammal on land and in the sea, whales included.

things.name: Farmed birds
things.more: Mostly chickens.

baron.title: The biomass distribution on Earth
baron.by: Yinon Bar-On, Rob Phillips and Ron Milo
baron.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115, 6506 (doi 10.1073/pnas.1711842115), free to read at Europe PMC

scale.note: Living things are weighed here by the carbon in them, the usual yardstick, because the water in a body varies. These are estimates: most are sure to within a few times, not to the last digit, and the paper gives the range for each.

guess.q: Which holds more living mass: every wild mammal on Earth, or all the people?
guess.after: People come to about 60 million tonnes of carbon. Every wild mammal on land and sea together comes to about 7 million. Livestock is larger again, about 100 million.

scale.title: From a blood cell to the next galaxy
scale.ask: Each thing is drawn as wide as it really is. No screen can hold them all at once, so walk from one to the next with Bigger and Smaller and watch each one turn into a speck beside its neighbour.

things.name: Red blood cell
things.more: About four times as wide as it is thick, and one of the smaller cells in your body.

things.name: A person
things.more: Dutch men born late last century, the tallest people measured, average just over 1.82 m. Most people are a little shorter.

things.name: Asteroid Bennu
things.more: A small asteroid that crosses Earth's path. A spacecraft brought a sample of it home.

things.name: Asteroid Vesta
things.more: One of the largest asteroids, 569 km at its longest.

things.name: Jupiter
things.more: The largest planet.

things.name: Betelgeuse
things.more: A red supergiant star in Orion. The paper puts its radius at 764 Suns, give or take about a hundred.

things.name: Neptune's orbit
things.more: The path of the farthest planet, 30 times as far from the Sun as Earth is.

things.name: To the nearest star
things.more: Proxima Centauri, 1.295 parsecs away. Light takes a little over four years to cross it.

things.name: The Milky Way
things.more: Our galaxy: about 100,000 light years across, and thin like a plate.

things.name: To the next big galaxy
things.more: The Andromeda galaxy, 765 kiloparsecs away, give or take 28.

guess.q: How many Earths would fit side by side across the Sun?
guess.after: About 109. The Sun is 1.39 million km across and the Earth is 12,700.

units.hook: Why can't a small count tell you much?

units.title: When the story does the thinking
units.outcome: Notice when a story is doing the thinking for you.
units.why: A good story feels true because it is well told, not because it is true. Whole countries have bet everything on a story everybody around them believed.
units.reachesYou: Every bubble works like this: tulips in 1637, houses in 2007, whatever is next. So do feeds that keep you angry. If everyone around you is sure, that is the moment to check.

main.title: Informing Ourselves to Death
main.by: Neil Postman on The Open Mind (1990)
main.licence: No licence stated; an Archive upload of the broadcast.
main.note: A teacher of forty years on what happens to thinking when information arrives faster than anyone can judge it. Said in 1990.

companions.title: The Tulipomania
companions.by: Charles Mackay, Extraordinary Popular Delusions (1841), read for LibriVox
companions.note: How a whole country came to trade houses for flower bulbs, told by a writer who saw the same thing happen again in his own time.

units.do: Think of one thing "everybody knows" in your circle. Write down where you first heard it and whether you ever saw it for yourself.

partials: Mackay tells of a single tulip bulb traded for a house.
Everyone's neighbour was getting rich, so it felt safe.
Postman: we now get more information than we can use or judge.
A feed shows you whatever keeps you watching.
When the price turned, everyone sold at once.
crystal.key: When everyone around you is sure all at once, slow down and check.

decoys.text: If a story feels true, it probably is.
decoys.why: The tulip buyers felt it too. A story feels true because it is well told.
Stories are how people remember anything. The skill is noticing when one is doing your thinking.

crystal.aha: A crowd that sets all at once traps its errors inside, the same as a crystal grown too fast.

map: the facts that fit the story

beats.say: Looks like a fun action movie.
The film is mostly slow, and sad.
News and ads cut trailers too.

units.needIt: Scams, rumors and family feuds run on stories that feel true; checking the story before you act on it saves money, friendships and sometimes your safety.

units.title: Changing your mind without shame
units.outcome: Change your mind in public without shame.
units.why: Being wrong is normal. Staying wrong to save face is what does the damage. The people we most admire for thinking clearly are the ones who said "I was wrong" out loud.
units.reachesYou: At work, at home, in a family argument that has run for years. The person who can say "I hadn't thought of that" ends up trusted.

main.title: The Ascent of Man, episode 11: Knowledge or Certainty
main.licence: On voidtv.net (its file is still in REVIEW there).
main.note: A mathematician stands at Auschwitz and says what happens when people believe they have absolute knowledge. The most quoted ending in television science.

companions.title: On Liberty, chapter 2 (first half): Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
companions.by: John Stuart Mill (1859), read for LibriVox
companions.note: Why even a wrong opinion should be heard: the person who only knows their own side of a case knows little even of that.

units.do: Pick one opinion you hold firmly. Write the strongest case against it you can, as if you believed it. Show it to someone who does believe it and ask if you got it right.

partials: Bronowski at Auschwitz: this is what people do when they are certain, with no test in reality.
Mill: whoever knows only their own side of a case knows little even of that.
Smiths heat steel and cool it slowly to make it stronger.
Scientists publish so other people can prove them wrong.
Saying "I was wrong" costs a moment. Staying wrong costs years.
crystal.key: Being wrong is the step before being right. Fixing it in the open is strength.

decoys.text: Never back down. It shows weakness.
decoys.why: That is how a flaw stays inside the crystal for good.
Changing your mind needs a reason, not just pressure. That is giving way, not annealing.

crystal.aha: Heat is not failure. Annealing is how a crystal, or a mind, comes out stronger.

beats.say: Your GPS plans a route home.
Your mind can work the same way.

units.needIt: Admitting a mistake early costs a little pride; defending it costs money, time and trust that grow every month you wait.

units.title: Find out for yourself
units.outcome: Read a hard text without an intermediary telling you what it means.
units.why: Knowing the name of a thing is not knowing the thing. Every summary is someone's choice of what to leave out, so the habit worth having is going to the source.
units.reachesYou: Your lease, your insurance policy, a law people are fighting about, a study a headline is quoting. The original is usually shorter and plainer than people assume.

main.title: The Pleasure of Finding Things Out
main.licence: No licence stated; an Archive upload of the broadcast, the same footing as VoidTV's shows.
main.note: A Nobel physicist on his father, the bird whose name tells you nothing about the bird, and why he would rather not know than be told.

companions.title: Fun to Imagine
companions.file: Richard P Feynman - FUN TO IMAGINE (full).mp4
companions.licence: No licence stated; an Archive upload of the broadcast.
companions.note: Ask him why magnets push each other apart and watch him refuse to give you an easy answer that isn't true.

companions.title: How to Read a Book
companions.licence: In copyright: we point you to a library copy rather than an upload.

units.do: Pick a short hard text you have only heard about: your lease, a founding document, a law in the news. Read it yourself first, then one summary, and write down where they differ.

partials: Feynman's father: knowing a bird's name in every language tells you nothing about the bird.
Feynman would not explain magnets with an easy answer that wasn't true.
Every summary is someone's choice of what to leave out.
Your lease is shorter and plainer than you think.
Adler: reading well is active. You ask the book questions.
crystal.key: Go to the source and build the understanding yourself. Then it is yours.

decoys.text: A good summary is as good as the original.
decoys.why: A summary is someone else's crystal, crushed to powder. You can't grow from powder.

decoys.text: Hard texts are only for experts.
decoys.why: Feynman's life says otherwise: an expert is someone who kept asking.

crystal.aha: Nobody handed you this one. You set it yourself, so you own it.

scene.analogy: A rumor at work, traced back

beats.say: At the start: he quit. Nobody fired him.

units.needIt: Your lease, your contract and the law in the news say exactly what they say; reading them yourself means nobody can tell you otherwise.

rosling.name: Hans Rosling

huff.name: Darrell Huff
huff.did: Wrote the most-read book on how statistics mislead.

postman.name: Neil Postman
postman.did: Forty years in the classroom; saw what television would do to public argument.

mackay.name: Charles Mackay
mackay.did: Chronicled the bubbles and manias of three centuries in 1841.

bronowski.name: Jacob Bronowski
bronowski.did: A working scientist who made The Ascent of Man.
